content: The diagnostic accuracy of the MSLAM-LAM and MLCwA tests is notably low. These tests demonstrate poor sensitivity but slightly better specificity. The study was conducted over five years in two endemic municipalities in the state of Pará, Brazil. Statistical methods included the kappa test to assess agreement between tests and the chi-squared test to evaluate differences between groups. The QUADAS-2 assessment for the study revealed the following: Domain 1 (Patient Selection): Low risk of bias and low concerns regarding applicability. Domain 2 (Index Tests): Unclear risk of bias with low concerns regarding applicability. Domain 3 (Reference Standard): Unclear risk of bias with low concerns regarding applicability. Domain 4 (Flow and Timing): Unclear risk of bias. The Sinha 2004 study evaluated the diagnostic performance of PGL1-O-BSA and 35kDa tests for leprosy. The study population included leprosy patients, doubtful cases, and individuals without leprosy. Patients were classified using the Indian Association of Leprosy (IAL) criteria. Doubtful cases were those not meeting all cardinal signs of leprosy, while the no leprosy group included household contacts and neighbors. The study enrolled 3,287 participants from three hyperendemic villages in India. The tests showed low sensitivity and specificity. The Stefani 2012 study compared antibody detection tests for diagnosing multibacillary (MB) leprosy. The ML Flow test using NTP-BSA was evaluated. Participants included newly diagnosed and untreated leprosy patients from Brazil and Nepal, household contacts of untreated MB patients, and healthy endemic controls. The study found that ML Flow had higher sensitivity for MB cases but lower sensitivity for paucibacillary (PB) cases. Specificity was higher among healthy controls. The Wang H 2015 study assessed ELISA NDO-BSA and MMP-II tests for MB and PB leprosy, household contacts, healthy controls, and tuberculosis (TB) patients. The study was conducted in Yunnan, Guizhou, and Sichuan provinces in China. Nested PCR showed comparable sensitivity to ELISA but higher specificity for detecting M. leprae. The Wen Yan 2014 study evaluated real-time PCR and nested PCR for diagnosing MB and PB leprosy. The study included 60 MB/PB cases, 32 controls with other skin conditions or healthy individuals, and 51 possible PB cases with only clinical symptoms. Real-time PCR demonstrated greater sensitivity and specificity compared to nested PCR. The evidence summary for ELISA targeting anti-MMP-II showed moderate sensitivity for MB cases but low sensitivity for PB cases. Specificity was variable across different groups, with higher specificity among healthy controls. Similarly, the NDO-LID lateral flow test demonstrated high sensitivity for MB cases but very low sensitivity for PB cases. Specificity was moderate to high across different groups. The ML Flow test showed high sensitivity for MB cases but low sensitivity for PB cases. Specificity was variable, with higher values among healthy controls. The diagnostic accuracy of these tests remains limited, particularly for PB leprosy. The literature search for PICO question 1b focused on identifying diagnostic tests for detecting M. leprae infection among contacts before the clinical diagnosis of leprosy. The search included studies published between 1996 and January 2017. Studies were required to report diagnostic accuracy based on sensitivity and specificity. Skin smear examinations and biopsies were excluded as they are part of the reference standard. Sensitivity and specificity were summarized using medians and ranges. The review highlighted the need for improved diagnostic tools with higher accuracy for early detection of leprosy.
